entries.seminar_title: Are Tariff Hikes Equal to Tariff Cuts?
entries.speaker: Hye Rim Yi
entries.abstract: It is well-documented that tariffs cause trade flows to fall. However, removing the same tariffs do not lead to trade flow recovery. I examine this asymmetry through the lens of US antidumping duties. I document that a tariff imposition causes an immediate drop in trade while the revocation of the same tariff does not result in increased trade. I examine this through the lens of a model with search costs in buyer and supplier relationships.

entries.seminar_title: Collective Decision-Making over Complex Decision Spaces
entries.speaker: Bailey Flanigan
entries.abstract:
Many societal decisions on which we want collective input — from allocating a public budget to deciding how an automated decision rule should behave — have enormous combinatorial spaces of possible outcomes. The standard approach to eliciting public input in such contexts is to elicit
element-level
 judgments (e.g., which decision rule output a person prefers at a
single input) and assume they suffice to reconstruct what people want. In this talk, I will present recent work (Flanigan & Si, EC 2026) showing that such elicitation methods fundamentally cannot identify preference structures that deal with global properties of the outcome, such as ensuring that a budget be balanced over impact categories, or that a decision rule treats like people alike. The preference model underlying this result, which generalizes standard choice models to represent priorities over the entire outcome space, also suggests a way forward: eliciting preferences at the level of
global priorities
rather than local judgements may recover richer preferences efficiently. I will illustrate this with ongoing work on participatory budgeting and discuss the questions it raises for the foundations of preference elicitation over complex decision spaces.
